## Protocol summary

### Input
One JSON object with `directory`, `accounts`, `gateways`, `jobs`.
- `directory`: canonical identity (sip:user@domain) -> array of aliases (normalized sip or tel URIs, ≤256 chars). Canonical identity is always an alias too. Aliases belong to exactly one identity. Normalize a parsed claim before lookup. Unknown claims are syntactically valid but have no directory identity.
- `accounts`: subject -> {"primary": identity, "allow": [identities]}. Primary implicitly allowed. Every account identity is a directory key.
- `gateways`: name -> {"local_domains": [domains], "peers": {name: [domains]}}. Domains are normalized canonical domains. A peer may assert identities only in its listed domains.
- Job: `gateway`, `ingress`, `trusted_out` (bool), and exactly one of `raw` or `source` (earlier job index). A source job contributes its forwarded wire text; if earlier job rejected, this rejects with `upstream`.
- Ingress: `{"kind":"local","subject":s}`, `{"kind":"peer","name":p}`, `{"kind":"untrusted"}`.

Limits: request text longer than 32768 chars → `syntax`, including reused forwarded request that grew during normalization.

URI grammar:

sip URI: `sip:USER@HOST`, scheme case-insensitive. USER: nonempty sequence of ASCII letters/digits and `- _ . ! ~ * ' ( ) +`, or `%HH` escapes. Each escape must decode to one of those permitted USER characters. Decode exactly once. USER case-sensitive. HOST: DNS name: dot-separated labels 1-63 of letters/digits/hyphens, each beginning and ending with letter/digit; max 253 chars before optional single trailing dot. Lowercase HOST, remove trailing dot. Escapes in HOST forbidden. No ports, params, passwords, queries, IPv4/IPv6 syntax, no sips.

Note USER chars: letters/digits and `- _ . ! ~ * ' ( ) +`. Note this set differs from token chars: USER allows `()` but not `%` literal... wait `%HH` escapes are allowed in USER, and `%` itself only as part of an escape. So a literal `%` not followed by two hex digits is invalid. Also USER allows `~ * ' ( ) + - _ .` and alnum. Not allowed: `!`? Wait: "- _ . ! ~ * ' ( ) +" — yes `!` is included. Let me list: `-`, `_`, `.`, `!`, `~`, `*`, `'`, `(`, `)`, `+`. Plus alnum. And `%HH` where decoded byte is in that set (alnum + those 10). Note: `%41` → 'A' allowed. `%20` → space not allowed. `%25` → '%' not allowed (since % isn't a permitted USER char). Decode exactly once — so `%2561` → decodes to "%61"... wait decode exactly once: `%2561` → '%','6','1'? `%25` decodes to '%', then "61" literal → user = "%61"? Hmm, "%61" contains '%' which is not a permitted USER char — but the rule says "Each escape must decode to one of those same permitted USER characters. Decode exactly once." So we decode each %HH once; the resulting characters must all be in the permitted set (alnum + `- _ . ! ~ * ' ( ) +`). Literal characters (non-escape) must also be in the permitted set. So after one decode, the resulting USER string must consist solely of permitted chars. `%2561` → decoded: '%' from %25, then '6','1' literals → '%' is not permitted → syntax error. Good — decode exactly once means we don't do a second pass to decode %61.

So algorithm: scan USER raw; build decoded string; for each char: if '%', must have 2 hex digits following, decode to byte c, c must be in permitted set; else char must be in permitted set. Non-ASCII? The whole request is ASCII already.

HOST: DNS name, labels 1-63 chars of [a-zA-Z0-9-], begin and end alnum. Max 253 chars before optional trailing dot. So host = labels joined by '.', optional single trailing '.' which is removed, then lowercase. Escapes (%HH) forbidden → '%' forbidden in host. Numeric labels allowed. What about a host that's all digits like `sip:a@123`? "A numeric DNS label is allowed; do not reinterpret it as an IP address." So `sip:a@123` is fine with host "123"? A single label of digits — allowed. What about `sip:a@1.2.3.4`? Labels "1","2","3","4" all valid DNS labels → allowed as DNS name, don't reject as IPv4. OK.

Max 253 characters before the trailing dot: the total host string length (excluding trailing dot) ≤ 253. And each label 1-63.

tel URI: `tel:+DIGITS`, scheme case-insensitive, 1-15 decimal digits, first nonzero. So `tel:+1...`. After '+' digits only, 1-15, first digit nonzero. `tel:+0123` → syntax (first digit zero). `tel:+` alone → syntax. `tel:+1234567890123456` (16 digits) → syntax.

"No whitespace occurs inside a URI." — URIs are parsed from values where whitespace would break parsing anyway.

The input `SIP:%65mber@STUDIO.TEST.` → normalized `sip:ember@studio.test`. So scheme → lowercase "sip"/"tel". USER preserved case-sensitive with escapes decoded. HOST lowercased, trailing dot removed.

Canonical identity keys in directory are like `sip:ember@studio.test` — normalized URIs. Normalized URI string form: `sip:` + user + `@` + host, or `tel:+` + digits. For lookup: build the normalized URI string and look it up in the alias map.

"The normalized URI `sip:anonymous@anonymous.invalid` is reserved, never a directory alias, and is valid only as a From or To value (or as a request URI). Using it in PPI/PAI/RPID is syntax." "Preserve validated From and To tags."

Now identity policy:

Validation order: first validate entire request grammar, including identity headers that will be stripped. Syntax failures take precedence.

Ingress local:
- Subject must exist (in accounts). If not → `unauthenticated`.
- Every nonanonymous From and any PPI must resolve to an allowed account identity whose canonical domain is hosted by this gateway.
  - "resolve to an allowed account identity" — the From/PPI claim (normalized URI) resolves via directory to a canonical identity; that identity must be in the account's allowed set (primary + allow); and its canonical domain must be in the gateway's local_domains.
  - "whose canonical domain is hosted by this gateway" — the canonical identity's domain (host part of the identity URI — is identity always sip? canonical identity is `sip:user@domain`, so yes sip). Domain = host part.
- Select PPI if present, otherwise nonanonymous From, otherwise the account primary.
- The selected identity must also be hosted and allowed. (If From/PPI checked, this is redundant except in the anonymous case where the primary is selected — primary must be hosted and allowed. Allowed: primary is implicitly allowed. Hosted: check domain.)
- PAI and RPID from local endpoint convey no authority and are ignored after syntax validation. So we don't check them against anything (except the anonymous-reserved syntax rule and grammar).

Failure classification: "Unknown local subjects, unknown peers, untrusted ingress, and a listed peer with no PAI reject with `unauthenticated`. Otherwise any failed lookup, authorization, hosting, peer authority, or identity agreement rejects with `identity`."

So local: subject not in accounts → unauthenticated. From fails to resolve to an account allowed identity or not hosted → identity. Anonymous From + primary not hosted → identity? The primary is implicitly allowed, but "The selected identity must also be hosted and allowed" — a failure there is a "failed lookup, authorization, hosting" → identity. Hmm, but wait — "Every account identity is a directory key", so the primary always resolves. So only hosting could fail → `identity`.

What if From is anonymous and there's no PPI → select primary. What if From is anonymous and PPI present → select PPI (PPI checked). Actually "Select PPI if present, otherwise nonanonymous From, otherwise the account primary." So order: PPI > nonanonymous From > primary.

For local: does the From/PPI check use the account of the ingress subject? Yes: "resolve to an allowed account identity" — the account for the subject.

Ingress peer:
- Peer must be listed (peer name in gateway's peers dict) — if not → `unauthenticated`.
- PAI must exist — if not → `unauthenticated`.
- All PAI claims must resolve to the same identity, within a domain in this peer's authority list.
  - Each PAI claim resolves via directory to a canonical identity. All must resolve to the same identity. If a claim fails to resolve (unknown) → `identity` ("any failed lookup... rejects with identity"). If they resolve to different identities → `identity` (identity agreement). The identity's domain must be in the peer's authority list (peers[gw][peer_name]) → else `identity` (peer authority).
- Every nonanonymous From, any PPI and any RPID must resolve to that same identity. Failed → `identity`.
- Anonymous From allowed.
- Select that asserted identity.

What if PAI addresses are 2 (sip+tel) that resolve to the same identity (aliases) → OK. That's example 13: PAI `<sip:ember@studio.test>, <tel:+12025550121>` both resolve to sip:ember@studio.test.

Note for peer: From/PPI/RPID must "resolve to that same identity" — resolve via directory. Anonymous From skips. PPI/RPID can't be anonymous (reserved URI in PPI/RPID is syntax).

Ingress untrusted: reject with `unauthenticated`, but only after full syntax validation! "First validate the entire request grammar... Syntax failures take precedence over authentication/identity failures." So for untrusted ingress with a syntactically invalid request → `syntax`? Hmm: "First validate the entire request grammar, including identity headers that will be stripped. Syntax failures take precedence over authentication/identity failures." Yes — syntax errors beat everything except `upstream`. What about text longer than 32768 → `syntax`. And what about upstream: "If that earlier job rejected, this job rejects with `upstream`." So upstream failure beats syntax? The source job contributes its forwarded text. If the earlier job rejected, there's no text at all → `upstream` regardless. Yes: job with source → if source rejected → `upstream` (without even looking at content, since there is none). If accepted, the forwarded wire text is the request to process (must be ≤32768 chars else syntax).

Wait: "Any request text longer than 32768 characters rejects with `syntax`, including a reused forwarded request that grew during normalization." So both raw and source text are checked for length > 32768 → syntax. Note "longer than 32768" → exactly 32768 is fine.

Hmm, for raw: is the length check before or after... raw is "a JSON string containing a whole request". Length in characters (Python str length). Note JSON input is decoded UTF-8; raw could contain non-ASCII chars → those are syntax errors anyway (non-ASCII anywhere). But length check first? If text > 32768 → syntax regardless. If non-ASCII and ≤32768 → also syntax. Either way syntax. Order doesn't matter since both give syntax.

But careful: the length check for source text "that grew during normalization" — the forwarded wire might be longer than the original raw. If > 32768 → syntax.
